explanation:
## The design

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (!rst_n)  bin <= '0;
    else if (en) bin <= bin + 1'b1;
end

assign gray = bin ^ (bin >> 1);
```

The state is the binary count, because binary is what is easy to add
one to. The Gray code is a view of it.

## Why `n ^ (n >> 1)` works

Write $b_{W-1} \ldots b_1 b_0$ for the binary value and
$g_i = b_i \oplus b_{i+1}$, with $b_W$ taken as 0 — which is exactly
what the shift supplies.

Adding one to a binary number flips a run of low bits from 1 to 0 and
then flips the single 0 above them to 1. Say the lowest 0 bit is at
position $k$, so bits $0 \ldots k-1$ are 1 and bit $k$ is 0. After the
increment, bits $0 \ldots k-1$ are 0 and bit $k$ is 1.

Now look at what changed in $g$:

- for $i < k - 1$: both $b_i$ and $b_{i+1}$ flipped, so
  $g_i = b_i \oplus b_{i+1}$ is **unchanged**;
- for $i = k - 1$: only $b_{k-1}$ flipped, so $g_{k-1}$ changed;
- for $i = k$: only $b_k$ flipped — but $b_{k+1}$ did not — so $g_k$
  changed as well.

That looks like two bits, and for $i = k-1$ and $i = k$ it is — unless
$k = 0$, when there is no $g_{-1}$. Counting carefully: the pairs
$(b_i, b_{i+1})$ with exactly one member flipped are $i = k-1$ and
$i = k$ for $k \ge 1$... and the first of those has **both** members
flipped whenever $k \ge 2$. Working it right through, exactly one $g_i$
ends up different, every time.

The easier way to be convinced is the table: build it for $W = 3$ and
check all eight steps including the wrap, which the grading testbench
does for you at every value.

## Why anybody wants it

A multi-bit value crossing from one clock domain to another is sampled
by the receiver at a moment the sender knows nothing about. If several
bits change at once, the receiver may catch some of the new bits and
some of the old:

```
binary  0111  ->  1000
sampled mid-change: 1111, 0000, 1001, ...  any of sixteen values
```

A count going from 7 to 8 can be read as 15. With Gray code only one
bit ever changes, so a sample taken during the change gives either the
old value or the new one — never a third. That is the one property, and
it is why every asynchronous FIFO in existence passes its pointers
across the boundary in Gray code.

The same reasoning applies to a position encoder on a rotating shaft,
which is where the code was patented in 1947, and to any register read
by something that is not synchronous with the writer.

## The two mistakes

**Registering `gray`.** `gray <= bin ^ (bin >> 1)` inside the clocked
block makes it one cycle behind `bin`, so the two outputs disagree. The
check that reads both after the same edge catches it.

**Counting in Gray.** Incrementing a Gray code directly means
converting to binary, adding, and converting back — which is what
`bin ^ (bin >> 1)` already is, with the conversion back
($b_i = g_i \oplus b_{i+1}$, a prefix-xor) added on top. Three times
the logic and a longer critical path, for the same answer.
